title: School Is a Word Game
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart describes a recurring classroom refrain, school is a word game, that he uses to reframe vocabulary and word-knowledge building as the engine behind reading comprehension and academic performance generally. He walks through concrete situations where he deploys the phrase: reassuring students that a low reading level score is really a vocabulary gap rather than a decoding problem, capturing novel words in the moment during class discussion, and running short vocabulary warm-ups. He connects the everyday practice to cognitive science, citing Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's argument that long-term memory, not working memory, is the central, dominant structure of human cognition, and pointing to a Nature video showing how word knowledge is distributed across the brain rather than stored in one place. The piece closes by generalizing the practical advice, teach words constantly across and beyond your discipline, into a broader claim about knowledge and human flourishing.
points: Reframes low reading level test results for students as a vocabulary problem rather than a decoding problem, once fluent decoding is confirmed — a specific diagnostic distinction teachers can use directly with struggling readers.
Gives a concrete low-friction vocabulary routine: notice unknown words in the moment, define them, log them in a running spiral-notebook list, and periodically revisit them.
Grounds the classroom practice in cognitive science, citing Kirschner et al.'s claim that long-term memory is the central, dominant structure of human cognition, not a passive repository.
Uses a Nature video on how word knowledge is stored as a constellation across the brain to argue that vocabulary-building is fundamentally knowledge-building, not a separate literacy skill.
quotes: When a student comes to me and reports that they "have a low reading level" based on an assessment like the SRI, I sit them down and share how these tests are essentially tests of vocabulary.

The one action step I want them to take moving forward, I say, is when they encounter a text and feel overwhelmed by the words they don't know, they need to switch gears and just focus on learning a few words from the text.

Our understanding of the role of long-term memory in human cognition has altered dramatically over the last few decades. It is no longer seen as a passive repository of discrete, isolated fragments of information that permit us to repeat what we have learned.

Rather, long-term memory is now viewed as the central, dominant structure of human cognition. Everything we see, hear, and think about is critically dependent on and influenced by our long-term memory.

So, very practically, do this if you want to empower young people and help cultivate in them stronger motivation: teach words! Those within your discipline, those outside of it; for fun, for seriousness, for the love of the game.
